title: The Consumption of Pink Slime Journalism: Who, What, When, Where, and Why?
screen_reason: Behavioural web-browsing study of a weighted national sample of American adults (N = 1,238; ~21 million website visits) during the 2020 US election, matched against domain lists of pink slime outlets (1,627 sites) and misinformation sites (1,796 sites). It reports population-level reach (share of American adults exposed to at least one site of each type), per-capita intensity of exposure among the exposed, and a news-diet share. These are core REACH and EXPOSURE estimates from behavioural data.

estimates.platform: Web browsing across computers, smartphones and tablets
estimates.measure_type: % of American adults who visited at least one misinformation website during the months surrounding the 2020 election
estimates.value_raw: 39.1% (95% CI = 36.4-41.8%) of Americans who were exposed to misinformation websites
estimates.denominator: 1,238 US adults in a YouGov browsing panel, weighted to be nationally representative, whose URL visits were passively collected from computers, smartphones and tablets (~21 million website visits)
estimates.definition: Participant visited at least one URL whose domain appears on a list of 1,796 misinformation sites, combining NewsGuard domains identified as 'repeatedly publishing false content' with sites identified in previous academic research as repeated purveyors of false information
estimates.misinfo_def: "a list of 1,796 misinformation sites compiled by Moore, Dahlke, and Hancock (2023), which combines websites NewsGuard identifies as 'repeatedly publishing false content' and websites identified in previous academic research as repeated purveyors of false information"
estimates.source_quote: While this number pales in comparison to the 39.1% (95% CI = 36.4-41.8%) of Americans who were exposed to misinformation websites (X(1) = 468.0, p < .001) and the 36.4% (95% CI = 33.7-39.1%) exposed to traditional local news websites (X(1) = 419.4, p < .001) during the same period, it is worth noting that for pink slime networks to be influential, they do not need to have broad reach necessarily.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Domain list of 1,796 misinformation sites from Moore, Dahlke and Hancock (2023): NewsGuard's 'repeatedly publishes false content' criterion (NewsGuard is described in the paper as 'an organization of professional journalists and editors who manually rate the quality of news websites') plus sites identified in prior academic research as repeated purveyors of false information. No per-article veracity judgement and no reliability statistic.
estimates.moderator_quote: We passively collected web browsing data (i.e., URLs visited) from computers, smartphones, and tablets via the survey company YouGov with 1,238 participants from August 24, 2020, to December 7, 2020, totaling 21 million website visits. [...] YouGov weighted participants to match a nationally-representative sample, and we use these weights in our analyses.
estimates.notes: This is the general misinformation reach estimate and the most poolable row in the paper: 39.1% of US adults visited at least one misinformation website in a ~3.5-month window. URL-based capture misses feed-based exposure without a click, so it is a lower bound for total exposure to misinformation content; conversely, source-level domain lists count every visit to a listed site regardless of whether the specific page was false, so it is an upper bound on exposure to actually false claims.

estimates.platform: Web browsing across computers, smartphones and tablets
estimates.measure_type: % of American adults who visited at least one pink slime (fake local news) website during the months surrounding the 2020 election
estimates.value_raw: 3.7% (95% CI = 2.8-5.0%) - about 1 in 25 - of American adults (~9.5 M people)
estimates.denominator: 1,238 US adults in a YouGov browsing panel, weighted to be nationally representative (~21 million website visits)
estimates.definition: Participant visited at least one URL whose domain appears on Bengani's (2022) list of 1,627 pink slime domains spanning five networks (three of which were active during the 2020 election: Metric Media, Star, Courier)
estimates.misinfo_def: "Pink slime journalism refers to organizations masquerading as local news, often serving special interests"; "organizations that mimic local news outlets but push partisan politics or corporate communications without following journalistic practices (e.g., not disclosing funding sources)"
estimates.source_quote: We estimate that 3.7% (95% CI = 2.8-5.0%)—about 1 in 25—of American adults were exposed to at least one pink slime website around the 2020 Election (August 24 - December 7, 2020).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Pink Slime: Who?', p. 7; also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Bengani (2022) pink slime domain list, described as 'the largest and most up-to-date list of pink slime web domains, spanning five networks (1,627 sites)'. Two of the five networks were created ahead of the 2022 midterms and so were not active in the 2020 window. No per-article coding and no reliability statistic.
estimates.moderator_quote: To identify visits to pink slime websites in our data, we used the largest and most up-to-date list of pink slime web domains, spanning five networks (Bengani 2022; 1,627 sites). Two networks in this list were created in the run-up to the 2022 midterms, but the other three were active during the 2020 US general election.
estimates.notes: borderline=true on construct scope, not on the number: pink slime outlets are defined by masquerading as local news and by opaque funding, not by publishing verifiably false claims, so this is exposure to a low-transparency partisan source class rather than to demonstrably false content. The paper itself argues pink slime should be conceptualised as distinct from misinformation ('consumption of the two types of content is quite different ... pink slime should be conceptualized as a unique phenomenon'). definition_variant=true because it is a different (narrower, differently defined) source-list variant of the misinformation reach row in the same country x platform cell; the two lists are separate and the rows should not be summed.

estimates.notes: Intensity, conditional on exposure (not a per-capita figure over the whole population). AMBIGUITY the adjudicator should see: the running text says 'exposed to 38.5 misinformation websites' and 'visited only 2.6 pink slime sites' (implying distinct sites), while the Figure 2 caption says the panel shows 'the number of visits'. I read it as number of visits to misinformation sites per exposed person, but distinct-site counts cannot be ruled out from the text.

The average participant exposed to at least one pink slime website visited only 2.6 (95% CI = 1.4–3.8) pink slime sites, significantly fewer than the average number of misinformation (t = −5.4, p < .001) and traditional local news sites visited (t = −4.6, p < .001) (see Figure 2A).

estimates.moderator_quote: Figure 2. [...] Panel B is the percentage of the news diet that the given website type makes up.
estimates.notes: News-diet share conditional on exposure, so it describes the diets of the 3.7% who saw any pink slime, not of all Americans; the population-wide diet share would be far smaller. The paper states that the equivalent misinformation diet share is significantly higher but never prints its value, so no misinformation diet-share row can be extracted. The paper does not define which domains count as 'news' in the denominator.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Traditional local news reach (36.4%, 95% CI 33.7-39.1%) and local news intensity (14.1 visits per exposed person) are the non-misinformation comparison condition and are not extracted. (2) Left- and right-leaning pink slime network sub-splits by party (Biden 3.6% vs Trump 0.5% for left-leaning networks; Biden 0.9% vs Trump 1.8% for right-leaning) are second-order subgroup-by-subgroup cells and were not extracted per R4 and the rule to keep the main figure. (3) Referrer shares (Google referred 23.4% of pink slime visits, Facebook 17.7%, Twitter 3.2%, YouTube 3.2%, webmail 2.5%, Bing 1.9%; Google referred 7.1% and Facebook 8.5% of misinformation visits) are shares of VISITS by referral channel, not shares of content or consumption that is misinformation, so they answer a different question and are not prevalence rows. (4) Table 1 topic percentages (e.g. 55.9% of consumed pink slime articles were Politics, 21.5% of produced pink slime articles were Gas Prices) are computed inside the pink-slime-only corpus and so are within-misinformation composition, not prevalence. (5) Average visit durations (54.7 s pink slime, 54.3 s misinformation, 57.4 s local news) and geo-distances (506.0 and 598.1 miles) are not shares. (6) The '~9.5 M people' population projection in the abstract is a derived headcount from the 3.7%, not an independent estimate. (7) Regression coefficients in Table 2 predicting exposure are associations, not prevalence. (8) The paper reports that the misinformation news-diet share is significantly larger than pink slime's 0.34% but never prints the value, so that row cannot be built.

rob.design: Passive URL-level web browsing collection via YouGov (YouGov Pulse) from computers, smartphones and tablets for 1,238 US adults, 24 August to 7 December 2020, totalling about 21 million website visits; YouGov survey weights applied throughout to approximate a nationally representative sample; informed consent and Stanford IRB approval (IRB-53941). Exposure classified at the domain level against three lists: pink slime (Bengani 2022, 1,627 sites), misinformation (Moore, Dahlke and Hancock 2023, 1,796 sites combining NewsGuard's 'repeatedly publishes false content' rating with academically identified purveyors), and local news (NewsGuard 'covers only local issues'). No response rate is reported for the panel. Authors' stated limitations: URL data miss feed-based exposure where users scroll without clicking; the sample skews older and whiter and the YouGov Pulse panel underrepresents non-high-school graduates and leans Democratic; and the 2020 window predates substantial growth in the pink slime networks. The regression models are fit on 1,056 of the 1,238 participants. Pink slime quantities rest on a very small number of events (32 pink slime visit observations in the geo-distance model versus 6,073 local news visits), so all pink slime confidence intervals are wide.
rob.item6_quote: To identify visits to misinformation websites, we use a list of 1,796 misinformation sites compiled by Moore, Dahlke, and Hancock (2023), which combines websites NewsGuard identifies as "repeatedly publishing false content" and websites identified in previous academic research as repeated purveyors of false information.
rob.item10_quote: We estimate that 3.7% (95% CI = 2.8-5.0%)—about 1 in 25—of American adults were exposed to at least one pink slime website around the 2020 Election (August 24 - December 7, 2020). While this number pales in comparison to the 39.1% (95% CI = 36.4-41.8%) of Americans who were exposed to misinformation websites.
